units.title: Unit I — Introduction to Computer Networks
units.content:
UNIT 1 — INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER NETWORKS

What is a Computer Network?

A computer network is a group of connected devices that can communicate and share data/resources.

Examples of devices:

  • Computers
  • Phones
  • Printers
  • Servers
  • Smart TVs

Why networks are used?

  • Share files
  • Share internet
  • Send messages/emails
  • Online gaming
  • Video calls
  • Cloud storage

Example: In a college lab, all computers are connected so students can share printers and internet.

Real-Life Uses of Computer Networks

  1. Internet

    The world’s biggest network. Used for: Browsing, YouTube, Social media, Online classes

  2. Online Shopping

    Apps/websites: Amazon, Flipkart. Need networks for: Payments, Product tracking, Communication

  3. Wearable Healthcare Systems

    Smart watches send health data through networks (e.g., heart rate monitoring, fitness tracking)

  4. Television

    Smart TVs use internet networks for Netflix, YouTube, OTT apps

  5. PAN (Personal Area Network)

    Small personal network around one person (e.g., Bluetooth headphones, Smartwatch connected to phone)

  6. Cloud Networks

    Stores data online instead of local computer (Google Drive, OneDrive)

Applications of Networks

  1. Communication — Email, WhatsApp, Video calling
  2. Data Sharing — Transfer files between systems (shared folder in office)
  3. Internet Access — Connects devices to global internet
  4. Cloud Computing — Remote applications and storage (Canva, Google Docs)
  5. IoT — Smart devices connected through internet (Alexa, Smart lights)
  6. Collaboration — Teams work together using shared resources (Google Meet, Microsoft Teams)

Components of Data Communication System

A communication system has 5 main parts:

  1. Sender — Device sending data (example: Computer)
  2. Receiver — Device receiving data (example: Mobile phone)
  3. Message — Actual data being sent (text, image, video)
  4. Transmission Medium — Path through which data travels (Cable, Wi-Fi, Fiber optics)
  5. Protocol — Rules for communication (HTTP, TCP/IP)

Data Flow Types

There are 3 communication modes:

  1. Simplex — Communication only in ONE direction (e.g., Keyboard → Computer, TV broadcast)
  2. Half-Duplex — Communication both ways but NOT at same time (e.g., Walkie-talkie)
  3. Full-Duplex — Communication both ways simultaneously (e.g., Mobile phone call)

Types of Networks

  1. LAN (Local Area Network) — Small-area network used in schools, offices, homes (high speed, low cost)
  2. MAN (Metropolitan Area Network) — Covers a city, connects many LANs
  3. WAN (Wide Area Network) — Large-area network, connects countries/world (example: Internet)
  4. PAN (Personal Area Network) — Very short-range network (Bluetooth, USB)
  5. WLAN (Wireless LAN) — Wireless version of LAN using Wi-Fi (home Wi-Fi, college Wi-Fi)

Internet Basics

The internet is a global network connecting millions of devices. Browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Edge) request web pages from web servers. A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is the address of a webpage (e.g., https://www.google.com). Domain names map to IP addresses. IP addresses can be IPv4 (192.168.1.1) or IPv6.

Packets

Data travels in small pieces called packets. Each packet contains source address, destination address, and actual data. Packets are reassembled at destination.

Network Hardware & Topologies

Topology = arrangement of network devices (physical vs logical). Types: Mesh, Star, Bus, Ring, Tree, Hybrid.

Mesh Topology

Every device connected to every other device. Very reliable but expensive.

Star Topology

All devices connect to central hub/switch. Most common topology.

Bus Topology

Single backbone cable connects all devices. Cheap but backbone failure stops network.

Ring Topology

Devices connected in circular form. Data travels in one direction.

Tree Topology

Combination of star and bus. Scalable and flexible.

Hybrid Topology

Combination of multiple topologies.

Connecting Devices

  1. Hub — Broadcasts data to all devices (Physical Layer)
  2. Switch — Sends data only to correct device using MAC addresses (Data Link Layer)
  3. Router — Connects different networks using IP addresses (Network Layer)
  4. Repeater — Regenerates weak signals

OSI Model

7 layers: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical. Each layer has specific responsibilities.

Final Summary: These lectures covered basics of computer networks, network types, internet concepts, topologies, networking devices, OSI model, TCP/IP model, addressing and protocols. Important for MCQs, viva, interviews, and exams.

units.title: Unit II — Data Communication & Networking
units.content:
UNIT 2 – DATA COMMUNICATION & NETWORKING NOTES (Easy Explanation)

I will explain all uploaded notes in very simple language without leaving any topic.

1. DATA AND SIGNALS

What is Data? Data means information. Examples: Text, Audio, Video, Images. Data can be Analog or Digital.

2. ANALOG AND DIGITAL DATA

Analog Data is continuous (e.g., human voice, temperature). Digital Data has discrete values (0 and 1) (e.g., computer data, keyboard input).

3. SIGNALS

To send data, it is converted into signals — electromagnetic waves carrying information. Signals can be analog (continuous sine waves) or digital (discrete levels, mostly 0 and 1).

4. PERIODIC AND NON-PERIODIC SIGNALS

Periodic: repeats after fixed time (sine wave). Non-periodic: does not repeat (internet data).

5. SINE WAVE

Important analog signal defined by amplitude, frequency, phase, wavelength.

6–10. AMPLITUDE, FREQUENCY, PERIOD, PHASE, WAVELENGTH

Amplitude = signal strength (volts). Frequency = cycles per second (Hz). Period = time for one cycle (seconds). Phase = position of waveform relative to time 0 (degrees/radians). Wavelength = distance traveled in one period (λ = vT).

11–14. FREQUENCY DOMAIN, COMPOSITE SIGNAL, BANDWIDTH

Frequency domain shows frequencies present. Composite signals are combinations of sine waves. Bandwidth = f_H − f_L (difference between highest and lowest frequency).

15–18. DIGITAL SIGNAL LEVELS, BIT RATE, BIT LENGTH, BASEBAND/BROADBAND

Digital signals may have various levels (2,4,8...). Bit rate = bits/sec. Bit length = propagation speed × bit duration. Baseband sends digital signal directly; broadband uses modulation to send over bandpass channels.

19–28. LINE CODING, CONVERSION, MODULATION

Line coding converts bits to electrical levels. Digital-to-analog uses ASK/FSK/PSK/QAM. ASK changes amplitude, FSK changes frequency, PSK changes phase, QAM combines ASK+PSK.

29–32. ANALOG-TO-ANALOG (AM/FM/PM)

AM changes carrier amplitude, FM changes carrier frequency, PM changes carrier phase.

33–38. MULTIPLEXING

Multiplexing shares a channel among users: MUX combines signals, DEMUX separates them. Types: FDM, TDM, WDM.

39–45. TRANSMISSION MEDIA

Guided (twisted pair, coaxial, optical fiber) and unguided (radio, microwave, infrared). Twisted pair is cheap; optical fiber uses light with very high speed.

46–48. DATA RATE LIMITS

Nyquist (noiseless): Bit rate = 2B log2 L. Shannon (noisy): Capacity = B log2(1+SNR).

49–52. PERFORMANCE TERMS

Bandwidth, Throughput, Latency. Latency includes propagation, transmission, queuing, processing delays. Propagation time = distance / propagation speed. Transmission time = message size / bandwidth.

Quick Difference Table

Analog vs Digital: continuous vs discrete, more noise vs less, examples voice vs computer data.

Very Important Exam Topics

Frequency, Period, Wavelength; Bandwidth; Bit rate vs Baud rate; ASK, FSK, PSK; AM, FM, PM; Multiplexing; Twisted pair vs Fiber optic; Nyquist Formula; Shannon Capacity; Propagation vs Transmission delay.

units.title: Unit III — Data Link Layer
units.content:
DATA LINK LAYER (DLL)

The Data Link Layer is the 2nd layer of the OSI model. Its main work is node-to-node delivery, framing, error control, flow control and media access control. It converts raw bits from the Physical Layer into organized frames.

Functions of Data Link Layer

  1. Framing — dividing data into small units called frames. Each frame contains source address, destination address, data and error-check bits. Framing separates messages and helps synchronization and error checking.

Types of Framing

Fixed Size Framing: every frame has same size (e.g., ATM). Advantage: simple. Disadvantage: wastes space for small data.
Variable Size Framing: frames vary in size and need start/end indicators. Methods: character-oriented and bit-oriented protocols.

Character-Oriented Protocol

Special bytes/characters are added as start and end flags. Problem: if same flag appears inside data — solved by Byte Stuffing (insert escape character before flag).

Bit-Oriented Protocol

Uses bit patterns (e.g., flag 01111110). Problem: same pattern inside data — solved by Bit Stuffing: after five consecutive 1s, insert a 0; receiver removes it.

Flow Control

Prevents fast sender from overwhelming slow receiver. Methods: Stop-and-Wait and Sliding Window.

Error Control

Error control detects and corrects errors. Types of errors: single-bit, multiple-bit, burst error (many bits corrupted over a span). Error detection uses redundancy bits; detection vs correction: detection only finds presence of error; correction locates and fixes it.

Error Detection Methods

Common methods: VRC (parity), LRC (two-dimensional parity), CRC (cyclic redundancy check), Checksum.

VRC (Vertical Redundancy Check)

Also called parity bit. Even or odd parity. Simple but cannot detect even number of errors.

LRC (Longitudinal Redundancy Check)

Column-wise parity (two-dimensional) — better at detecting burst errors.

CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check)

Polynomial-based method used in Ethernet, Wi‑Fi. Sender appends remainder of polynomial division; receiver divides to check remainder. Detects single-bit, double-bit, and many burst errors (detection only).

Checksum

Divide data into sections, add them, take complement and send checksum. Receiver adds sections plus checksum — if result is all 1s, accept. Used in IP/TCP/UDP.

Error Correction

Methods: retransmission (ARQ) and error-correcting codes (e.g., Hamming code). Hamming code places redundancy bits at powers of two positions to detect and correct single-bit errors. Formula: 2^r >= m + r + 1 determines required parity bits.

ARQ Protocols

Stop-and-Wait: send one frame, wait for ACK; simple but slow. Uses timer and sequence numbers (modulo-2).
Go-Back-N ARQ: sender can send multiple frames (sliding window); if an error occurs, sender retransmits from erroneous frame onward. Window size = 2^m − 1.
Selective Repeat ARQ: only erroneous frames retransmitted; receiver stores correct frames; more efficient; window size condition ≤ 2^{m−1}.

Ethernet & MAC

Ethernet is IEEE 802.3 LAN technology. Ethernet frame contains preamble, destination MAC, source MAC, type, data and CRC. Minimum frame size = 64 bytes, maximum = 1518 bytes. MAC address is 48-bit physical address (hex), e.g., AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF. Types: unicast (LSB of first byte = 0), multicast (LSB = 1), broadcast (all bits = 1).

Multiple Access Control (MAC Sublayer)

DLL is divided into LLC and MAC sublayers. MAC controls who can use the transmission medium.

Random Access

All stations compete; no central controller. Protocols: ALOHA (Pure and Slotted), CSMA, CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA.

Pure ALOHA: transmit anytime; max throughput ≈ 18.4%.
Slotted ALOHA: time divided into slots; max throughput ≈ 36.8%.

CSMA

Carrier Sense Multiple Access: sense channel before sending. Persistence methods: 1-persistent, non-persistent, p-persistent. CSMA/CD (collision detection) used in Ethernet; CSMA/CA (collision avoidance) used in Wi‑Fi (uses IFS, backoff timers, ACKs).

Controlled Access

Only one station transmits at a time via reservation, polling, or token passing.

Important Exam Points

  • Bit Stuffing: after five 1s insert 0
  • Go-Back-N window size: 2^m − 1
  • Selective Repeat window: 2^{m−1}
  • CRC: best error detection method
  • CSMA/CD used in Ethernet; CSMA/CA used in Wi‑Fi
  • Slotted ALOHA throughput 36.8%; Pure ALOHA throughput 18.4%

units.title: Unit IV — Network Layer – IP Addressing
units.content:
Unit: Network Layer – IP Addressing

1. Introduction to Network Layer

The Network Layer is the 3rd layer of the OSI model. Its main job is to deliver packets from the source network to the destination network.

Main Functions: Logical addressing (IP addressing), Routing, Packet forwarding, Fragmentation, Congestion handling, Internetworking. Devices: Router, Layer-3 Switch.

2. Network Layer Design Issues

Problems and requirements include store-and-forward packet switching, services provided to transport layer (connectionless vs connection-oriented), routing (static/dynamic), and implementation details.

a) Store-and-Forward Packet Switching

Router stores the packet, checks destination and forwards to next router. Steps: Receive, Store, Check header, Forward. Advantage: reliable. Disadvantage: increased delay.

b) Services Provided to Transport Layer

Connectionless Service: no setup, each packet independent (example: IP). Fast but less reliable. Connection-Oriented Service: setup required, fixed path, reliable but more overhead.

c) Implementation of Connectionless Service

Uses datagram packets; each router decides route independently (IP protocol).

d) Implementation of Connection-Oriented Service

Uses virtual circuits with phases: setup, data transfer, connection release.

e) Routing

Selecting best path: goals include minimum delay and congestion. Types: static and dynamic routing.

3. IP Addressing

IP Address is a logical address assigned to every device. Purpose: identify host and network and help routing.

4. IPv4 Address

IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses divided into 4 octets (example: 192.168.1.1). Structure: Network ID + Host ID.

5. Classful Addressing

Addresses divided into classes:

  • Class A: 1.0.0.0 – 126.255.255.255, default mask 255.0.0.0, format N.H.H.H, ~126 networks, ~16 million hosts.
  • Class B: 128.0.0.0 – 191.255.255.255, mask 255.255.0.0, format N.N.H.H, ~65,534 hosts.
  • Class C: 192.0.0.0 – 223.255.255.255, mask 255.255.255.0, format N.N.N.H, ~254 hosts.
  • Class D: 224.0.0.0 – 239.255.255.255 (multicast).
  • Class E: 240.0.0.0 – 255.255.255.255 (experimental).

6. Classless Addressing (CIDR)

CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) uses IP/prefix notation (e.g., 192.168.1.0/24). Advantages: efficient allocation, reduced routing table size, supports variable-size networks.

7. Subnetting

Subnetting divides a large network into smaller networks for management, reduced traffic and improved security. Number of subnets = 2^n (n = borrowed bits). Number of hosts = 2^h − 2 (h = host bits). Example: 192.168.1.0/24 → need 4 subnets → borrow 2 bits → new prefix /26 → mask 255.255.255.192 → subnets: 0–63, 64–127, 128–191, 192–255.

8. Supernetting

Supernetting combines smaller networks into one larger network to reduce routing entries (e.g., combine 192.168.0.0/24 and 192.168.1.0/24 → 192.168.0.0/23).

9. Network Layer Services

  • Packetizing — converts data into packets.
  • Routing — selects best path.
  • Forwarding — moves packets to next router.
  • Internetworking — connects different networks.
  • Congestion Control — controls excessive traffic.
  • Error Handling — detects packet problems.

10. Network Layer Performance

Performance metrics: Throughput (data/time), Delay (transmission, propagation, processing, queuing), Jitter (variation in delay), Packet Loss.

11. Forwarding of IP Packets

Forwarding steps: receive packet, check destination IP, search routing table, select next hop, forward packet. Example forwarding table maps destination networks to next hops.

12. IP Header (IPv4 Header)

Fields: Version, Header Length, Type of Service, Total Length, Identification, Flags, Fragment Offset, TTL (Time To Live), Protocol (TCP=6, UDP=17, ICMP=1), Header Checksum, Source Address, Destination Address.

13. IPv6 Addressing

IPv6: 128-bit address, large address space, improved routing and security, no broadcast. Example: 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334. Rules: remove leading zeros; use :: for consecutive zero groups.

14. IPv4 vs IPv6

IPv4 is 32-bit, IPv6 is 128-bit; IPv6 has larger address space and built-in security features; IPv4 uses decimal notation, IPv6 uses hexadecimal.

15. Short Notes

Datagram: independent packets. Virtual Circuit: predefined path. Fragmentation: breaking large packets. Routing Table: used by routers to determine next hop.

units.title: Unit V — Network Layer: Routing & Congestion Control
units.content:
Unit Notes: Network Layer – Routing & Congestion Control

1. Network Layer Overview

The Network Layer is the 3rd layer of the OSI model. Its main job is to deliver packets from source to destination across multiple networks, decide best path using routing algorithms, and handle congestion. Main functions: Logical addressing (IP Address), Routing, Packet forwarding, Congestion control, Fragmentation and reassembly.

PART A — ROUTING

2. Routing

Routing selects the best path for sending packets. Routers use routing algorithms to determine paths.

3. Routing Algorithms

Routing algorithms decide which path packets should follow and how routers exchange routing information.

Types of Routing Algorithms

  1. Static Routing: manually configured, simple, secure, low overhead, but not scalable.
  2. Dynamic Routing: routers automatically update tables, adapts to changes, used in large networks; more CPU and bandwidth usage.

4. Shortest Path Algorithm

Finds minimum-cost path. Cost may depend on distance, delay, bandwidth, hop count. Dijkstra’s algorithm is used in link-state routing (OSPF). Steps: start from source, assign distances, select nearest unvisited, update neighbors, repeat. Advantages: accurate shortest path and fast convergence; Disadvantages: requires full network info and high memory.

5. Distance Vector Routing

Routers share routing tables with neighbors. Each router maintains destination, distance, next hop. Uses Bellman-Ford equation. Routers periodically exchange tables and update. Advantages: simple, low computation. Disadvantages: slow convergence, routing loops, count-to-infinity problem (mitigations: split horizon, poison reverse, hold-down timers).

6. Link State Routing

Each router has full topology information. Steps: discover neighbors, measure link costs, create Link State Packet (LSP), flood LSPs, build topology database, run Dijkstra. Features: fast convergence, accurate routing, no loops; Disadvantages: complex, more memory/CPU.

7. Unicast Routing Protocols

Examples: RIP (Distance Vector, hop count metric, max hops 15, UDP port 520), OSPF (Link State, uses Dijkstra, hierarchical, fast convergence), BGP (Path Vector, used between autonomous systems, policy-based).

PART B — CONGESTION CONTROL

8. Congestion Control

Congestion occurs when traffic exceeds capacity, causing packet loss, delay and reduced performance. Causes: too much traffic, slow routers, limited bandwidth, buffer overflow, high retransmissions.

9. Congestion Control Algorithms

Two broad types:

  1. Open Loop (Prevention): techniques to avoid congestion before it happens (retransmission policy, window policy, acknowledgment policy, discarding policy, admission control).
  2. Closed Loop (Feedback): detect congestion and inform sender to adjust rate (backpressure, choke packet, implicit signaling, explicit signaling).

10. Traffic Shaping Algorithms

Leaky Bucket: packets enter at any rate, leave at fixed rate; overflow packets discarded — smoothes traffic but not good for bursts. Token Bucket: tokens generated at fixed rate; packet sent only if token available — allows burst traffic and is more flexible.

11. QoS (Quality of Service)

QoS ensures better service for important traffic. Parameters: Bandwidth, Delay, Jitter, Reliability.

units.title: Unit VI — Transport Layer, Application Layer & Recent Trends
units.content:
Unit Notes – Transport Layer, Application Layer & Recent Trends in Computer Networks

1. Transport Layer

The Transport Layer is the 4th layer of the OSI model and provides communication between applications running on different devices.

Functions of Transport Layer

  • Process-to-process communication
  • Segmentation and reassembly
  • Error detection and recovery
  • Flow control
  • Multiplexing and demultiplexing
  • Reliable data transfer
  • Congestion control

Transport Layer Services

1. Process-to-Process Delivery

Ensures data reaches the correct application process using port numbers. Example: Browser uses port 80 or 443; Email uses port 25.

2. Segmentation and Reassembly

Breaks large data into smaller segments; receiver reassembles segments. Advantages: faster transmission and efficient communication.

3. Flow Control

Controls data transfer speed between sender and receiver to prevent receiver overload. Example: TCP sliding window mechanism.

4. Error Control

Checks for lost packets, duplicate packets and corrupted packets using checksum, acknowledgment and retransmission.

5. Multiplexing and Demultiplexing

Multiplexing combines data from multiple applications; demultiplexing separates received data for the correct applications.

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)

TCP is connection-oriented, reliable and error-checked. Used in web browsing, email and file transfer.

Features of TCP

  • Reliable delivery
  • Ordered delivery
  • Error recovery
  • Flow control
  • Congestion control

TCP Header Format

Main fields include Source Port, Destination Port, Sequence Number, Acknowledgment Number, Header Length, Flags, Window Size, Checksum, Urgent Pointer and Options.

TCP Flags

  • SYN – Start connection
  • ACK – Acknowledgment
  • FIN – Finish connection
  • RST – Reset connection
  • PSH – Push data immediately
  • URG – Urgent data

TCP Three-Way Handshake

Used to establish connection: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. TCP connection termination uses FIN and ACK flags in four steps.

UDP (User Datagram Protocol)

UDP is connectionless, faster and unreliable. Used in video streaming, online gaming and DNS.

Features of UDP

  • No connection setup
  • Low overhead
  • Faster transmission
  • No error recovery

UDP Header Format

Fields include Source Port, Destination Port, Length and Checksum.

TCP vs UDP

FeatureTCPUDP
ConnectionConnection-orientedConnectionless
ReliabilityReliableUnreliable
SpeedSlowerFaster
Error RecoveryYesNo
OrderingMaintainedNot maintained
UsageWeb, EmailStreaming, Gaming

2. Application Layer

The Application Layer is the top layer of the OSI model and provides services directly to users.

Services of Application Layer

  • File transfer
  • Email service
  • Web browsing
  • Name services
  • Remote login
  • Domain Name System (DNS)

DNS

DNS converts domain names into IP addresses. Example: google.com → 142.250.x.x.

Features of DNS

  • Hierarchical system
  • Distributed database
  • Fast name resolution

DNS Components

  • DNS Resolver – client-side DNS query tool
  • Root Server – top-level server
  • TLD Server – handles .com, .org, .edu
  • Authoritative Server – contains actual IP records

DNS Working Process

  1. User enters website name
  2. Resolver checks cache
  3. Query sent to root server
  4. Root directs to TLD server
  5. TLD directs to authoritative server
  6. IP address returned
  7. Browser opens website

DNS Record Types

RecordPurpose
AMaps name to IPv4
AAAAMaps name to IPv6
MXMail server
CNAMEAlias
NSName server

E-Mail

Electronic mail system used for communication.

Components of E-Mail System

  • User Agent (UA) – used to compose and read email, examples: Gmail, Outlook
  • Mail Transfer Agent (MTA) – transfers email between servers using SMTP
  • Mail Access Agent (MAA) – retrieves email from server using POP3/IMAP

Email Protocols

ProtocolPurpose
SMTPSend email
POP3Download email
IMAPAccess email online

Working of E-Mail

  1. User writes email
  2. SMTP sends mail
  3. Mail server stores email
  4. Receiver accesses using POP3/IMAP

FTP (File Transfer Protocol)

FTP transfers files between computers.

Features of FTP

  • Upload/download files
  • Authentication support
  • File management

FTP Components

  • FTP Client – requests files
  • FTP Server – stores files

FTP Connections

  • Control Connection – used for commands (Port 21)
  • Data Connection – used for file transfer (Port 20)

FTP Working

  1. Client connects to FTP server
  2. User authentication
  3. Commands exchanged
  4. File transfer occurs

Advantages of FTP

  • Fast file transfer
  • Large file support
  • Remote file access

Disadvantages of FTP

  • Less secure without encryption
  • Plain-text authentication

3. Recent Trends in Computer Networks

SD-WAN

SD-WAN is a modern WAN architecture controlled by software.

Features of SD-WAN

  • Centralized management
  • Intelligent traffic routing
  • Better performance
  • Reduced cost
  • Cloud integration

SD-WAN uses software controller, dynamically selects best network path, and prioritizes important traffic.

Advantages of SD-WAN

  • Improved application performance
  • Easy management
  • Better security
  • Lower operational cost

CDN (Content Delivery Network)

CDN is a distributed network of servers used to deliver web content quickly.

Purpose of CDN

  • Reduce latency
  • Faster content delivery
  • Improve website performance

How CDN Works

Content stored on multiple servers; user request goes to nearest server; content delivered quickly.

Features of CDN

  • Caching
  • Load balancing
  • High availability
  • DDoS protection

Advantages of CDN

  • Faster loading
  • Reduced bandwidth usage
  • Better user experience
  • Increased reliability

Applications of CDN

  • Video streaming
  • Online gaming
  • E-commerce
  • Social media
  • Cloud applications

Difference Between SD-WAN and CDN

SD-WANCDN
Manages WAN trafficDelivers content faster
Used in enterprise networksUsed for web acceleration
Focus on routingFocus on caching
Improves connectivityImproves content delivery

Important Short Notes

  • TCP – Reliable transport protocol.
  • UDP – Fast but unreliable protocol.
  • DNS – Converts domain names into IP addresses.
  • FTP – Transfers files over network.
  • SD-WAN – Software-controlled WAN technology.
  • CDN – Distributed servers for faster content delivery.
